cert_revocation.ocsp_refused: OCSP response refused by the authority ({reason})
cert_revocation.score_cap: The site certificate has been revoked by its certificate authority
cert_revocation.score_must_staple: Must-Staple certificate without an OCSP staple
cert_revocation.score_no_info: No revocation information in the certificate

finding.cert_revocation.must_staple_miss: The certificate requires an OCSP staple (Must-Staple) but the server sends none: the site will be unreachable for browsers that enforce it.
finding.cert_revocation.no_revocation_in: The certificate lists neither an OCSP responder nor a certificate revocation list (CRL): its revocation could not be checked.
finding.cert_revocation.revoked: The site certificate has been revoked by its certificate authority: clients that check revocation reject it. Replace it immediately.
finding.cert_revocation.stale_staple: The OCSP staple sent by the server is stale: enable its automatic renewal.
finding.cert_revocation.unverifiable: The revocation status could not be confirmed by any source (authority unreachable or stale response).
module.cert_revocation.checks: Checks that the certificate has not been revoked: OCSP staple attached by the server, query to the authority's OCSP responder (response and signature verified) and certificate revocation list (CRL) as a fallback. Flags a Must-Staple certificate without a staple and the absence of any revocation information.
module.cert_revocation.fix:
If the certificate is revoked: replace it immediately. Generate a NEW private key (the old one may be compromised: never reuse it), request a new certificate from the authority, install it with its full chain and reload the server.
If the revocation followed a key leak: remove the old private key from every place it may lie around (backups, code repositories, test servers, shares, old servers) and find out how it leaked. If the revocation is unexpected, ask the authority for the reason.
If the certificate is Must-Staple but has no staple: enable OCSP stapling on the server (see the snippet) or reissue the certificate without the Must-Staple extension. Let's Encrypt ended OCSP in 2025 and now rejects Must-Staple: remove that option from the ACME client configuration.
If the staple is stale: check that the server reaches the authority's OCSP responder (outbound HTTP allowed by the firewall, `resolver` set on nginx, `SSLStaplingCache` set on Apache), then reload the server. If the authority no longer has an OCSP responder, do not enable stapling.
If the certificate lists neither OCSP nor a certificate revocation list (CRL): reissue it from a recognised public authority, whose certificates include one of the two.
If the status could not be confirmed: run the scan again later (the authority may have been unreachable). If it persists, read the responder address with `openssl x509 -in cert.pem -noout -ocsp_uri` and check that it answers.
Check the staple: `openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com -status` must show "OCSP Response Status: successful" then "Cert Status: good". Then run the scan again.
module.cert_revocation.title: Certificate revocation (OCSP and CRL)
module.cert_revocation.why: A revoked certificate (stolen key, wrongful issuance) is still accepted by clients that do not check: monitoring it lets you replace a compromised certificate without delay.
